3.1 SAMPLE SELECTION


My ideal sample consists of firms with flat earnings followed by significant
earnings increases for an extended period during which the firms would
not experience any significant events that might affect disclosure. Disclosure during the flat earnings period will be used as a benchmark against
which to compare increased earnings disclosure. Some portion of these
firms will experience eventual declines in earnings, enabling me to investigate disclosure changes through the entire earnings life cycle.

With this ideal as a guide, I screen firms on a number of dimensions using
data from the 1996 Compustat quarterly tapes (see table 1 for a tabulation of
these criteria and their impact). To mitigate the risk of a time-period specific
shock, I identify firms over a period of 13 years (1980–1993). This period
also overlaps the majority of prior empirical disclosure work, increasing the
present paper’s comparability with previous work. During this period, there
are 25,280 firm-period observations, consisting of 2,544 individual firms,
with the necessary data items available on Compustat. <sup>7</sup>

I next require all firms to have eight contiguous quarters of increases in
seasonally adjusted earnings before extraordinary items (i.e., current year
Compustat Quarterly Data Item #25 less the same data item for the same
quarter of the prior year). <sup>8</sup> To enhance comparability across firms, I deflate all earnings by total assets at the beginning of the first quarter of increased earnings. Requiring quarterly increases, rather than annual, avoids
conflicting signals within the increase time period. <sup>9</sup> Requiring eight contiguous quarters also helps to assure that the period of earnings increases
is sufficiently long to activate the incentives for disclosure discussed in the
hypotheses section. To ensure relatively flat earnings in the benchmark period, I require the sum of the absolute values of the changes in deflated
earnings during the benchmark year to be less than or equal to .02. <sup>10</sup> The
1,096 firm-period observations that meet these criteria are derived from 364
individual firms. As shown in table 1, requiring this unique earnings pattern
is clearly the most restrictive criteria in developing my sample. However, it
is exactly this earnings pattern that will allow me to perform a powerful and
clear analysis of the relation between earnings changes and disclosure.

7 A firm-period observation includes 20 quarters of information: the 4 quarters of the
benchmark period, the 8 quarters of the earnings increase period, and 8 subsequent quarters.

8 For many of the criteria used in the sample selection process, there is no theory that
provides an exact cutoff point for excluding a firm. Cutoffs were created with the joint goal of
reducing threats to the validity of the tests and collecting a sample with a reasonable number
of observations and cross-sectional make-up.

9 Samples based on annual earnings include firm-quarters with earnings decreases during
the “increased earnings” period. Thus, management might consider a portion of the time
period being studied as bad news.
